content: QH-II-66, also referred to as QH-ii-066, is a sedative drug that belongs to the benzodiazepine class. It exerts effects similar to other benzodiazepines but demonstrates a significantly higher degree of selectivity compared to most drugs in this category. As a result, it induces less sedation and ataxia than related compounds such as diazepam and triazolam, while still retaining anticonvulsant properties. QH-ii-066 functions as a highly subtype-selective agonist of GABA-A receptors. It was specifically designed to bind selectively to the α5 subtype of GABA-A receptors. The α5 subtype, along with the α1 subtype to a lesser extent, represents one of the primary targets in the brain responsible for mediating the effects of alcohol. Consequently, one of the objectives behind the development of QH-ii-066 was to replicate the GABAergic effects of alcohol while isolating these effects from other actions. This compound mimics certain effects of alcohol, such as sedation and ataxia, but does not enhance appetite. This distinction is likely because the appetite-stimulating effects of alcohol are mediated by the α1 subtype of GABA-A receptors rather than the α5 subtype. Additionally, it is noteworthy that the inverse agonist Ro15-4513, which blocks the α4 subtype of GABA-A receptors, has been shown to reverse the effects of alcohol. This observation suggests that the α4 subtype also plays a significant role in producing the subjective effects associated with alcohol intoxication.
